# Linux Server Ops Gotchas

> Known Linux service-management, packaging and desktop-session patterns (systemd, daemons, package updates, X11/Wayland) that cause silent failures or hard-to-debug outages. Load HIGH entries before working on Linux server services, distro packaging, or screen capture.

## Entries

- [Daemon stays dead after an auto-upgrade restart (socket bind race + Restart=on-abort)](systemd-restart-on-abort-bind-race.md): unattended-upgrades + needrestart restarts a daemon; the new master loses the port-bind race and the packaged Restart=on-abort policy leaves it failed with no retry. Connection-refused until manual restart/reboot. HIGH.
- [systemd 203/EXEC on unit scripts under /home (SELinux user_home_t)](selinux-systemd-exec-home.md): SELinux blocks systemd from exec'ing ExecStart scripts living under /home; `mv` into /etc/systemd/system also preserves the wrong label so the unit won't load. Use /opt or /usr/local/bin and `restorecon`. MEDIUM.
- [Post-reboot verification that only checks the front door misses units that died at boot](post-reboot-verify-failed-units.md): closing on "the web server returns 200" proves nothing about application units behind it; a unit that fails seconds into boot stays invisible and journald rotation later erases the error. Baseline `systemctl list-units --failed` before the reboot and diff after. HIGH.
- [XWayland reports a viewable root window of the right size and still refuses XGetImage](xwayland-root-window-holds-no-pixels.md): on an XWayland session `XGetGeometry` returns the full multi-monitor size, `map_state` is IsViewable and depth is 24 -- and `XGetImage` returns BadMatch for *any* region, including 100x100 at the origin, because XWayland never composites native Wayland surfaces into the X root. Every pre-flight check passes, so it does not read as a capture problem; clamping the rectangle (the normal BadMatch fix) changes nothing and sends you hunting a second bug. The trap that gets you here is that XWayland sets BOTH `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` and `DISPLAY`, so detection that tests `DISPLAY` first -- the obvious order -- picks X11 on a Wayland desktop, connects successfully and captures nothing, which looks like a driver or permissions fault on the customer's machine. Test `XDG_SESSION_TYPE`, then `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, then `DISPLAY`, and use the xdg-desktop-portal ScreenCast path on Wayland (which always prompts a human -- there is no unattended route). Verified against a real compositor. HIGH.
- [Xlib's default X error handler calls exit(), so one protocol error kills your daemon](xlib-default-error-handler-exits.md): Xlib's default handler prints to stderr and calls `exit(1)` from inside a library, on whichever thread made the call. A single BadMatch, BadDrawable or BadWindow -- an unplugged monitor, a window closing between two calls, a display server restart -- terminates the whole process with no panic, no stack trace, and no line in your own log, because the handler exits before returning to your call site. The message goes to stderr rather than your logger, so under a systemd unit it lands in the journal while the app log just stops; under `Restart=always` the symptom is a service that "restarts occasionally". Install `XSetErrorHandler` (process-global, gate with sync.Once) before the first X call, and `XSync` before reading the flag or an async error gets blamed on the next call. `XSetIOErrorHandler` is the second, separate fatal path. HIGH.
- [dpkg, rpm and pacman each signal "this is an upgrade" differently, and guessing disables the service on the two you did not test](maintainer-script-upgrade-detection.md): dpkg passes `$1 == "upgrade"`, rpm passes the number of packages that will REMAIN (`1` = upgrade, `0` = removal -- the opposite of the intuitive reading), and pacman does not call `pre_remove` on an upgrade at all. A script written and tested on Debian takes the removal branch on every rpm upgrade and runs `systemctl disable`: the upgrade succeeds, `rpm -q` shows the new version, and the service is switched off and will not survive a reboot. Nothing errors and the exit status is 0, so a fleet goes quiet one distro family at a time and the affected machines look identical to ones that are powered down. Match `upgrade|1` in one case statement, stop unconditionally but disable only on real removal, use `try-restart` in post-install (or the old binary runs until the next reboot), and write the scripts in `/bin/sh` -- rpm and pacman scriptlets run under dash. HIGH.
